analysis.tldr: A potential severe weather event called a Super El Nino could disrupt crops and push up your grocery bills by 2027.
the_story: India's food industry is warning about a potential supply shock projected for the year 2027.
Experts say a Super El Nino may disrupt crop production and elevate food inflation (rising prices of everyday goods).
There are growing concerns about the impact on sugar and oilseed production, especially in states with severe drought conditions.
The livestock sector is also preparing for increased feed costs due to these challenges.
analysis.what_happened: India's food industry is sounding the alarm about a Super El Nino expected in 2027. This weather pattern is projected to disrupt crop production and cause drought conditions, leading to fears of lower supplies and higher food prices.
analysis.analogy: It is like a severe drought drying up a farmer's well, meaning fewer vegetables grow, forcing the local vegetable market to charge much higher prices for whatever is left.
why_it_matters_india: A Super El Nino disrupts crop production and creates severe drought conditions in parts of India.
Lower harvests of sugar and oilseeds lead to a drop in food supply.
Scarcity pushes food inflation higher, raising grocery and household expenses for everyday citizens.
Higher food prices can force the RBI (Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank) to keep interest rates higher for longer to control inflation.

impacts.rationale: Higher food and feed costs mean everyday items become costlier, which is bad for household budgets.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: If inflation stays high, the government may have to pay higher interest rates to borrow money, which can make loans costlier for regular people.

watch_next: Weather updates regarding the arrival and strength of the El Nino pattern
Updates on sugar and oilseed crop yields from drought-prone states
analysis.caveats: Weather predictions made years in advance can change, and future agricultural measures could soften the blow.

Investors buy gold as a safe asset during political trouble, raising local prices, which is good for existing gold owners but bad for buyers.

analysis.tldr: Strong domestic tax collections are good for government spending, but growing reliance on imports could mean local manufacturing needs a closer look to protect local jobs.
the_story: India's Goods and Services Tax (GST, a unified indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services) collections rose to Rs 2.04 lakh crore in September, showing strong overall numbers.
Tax experts pointed out a wide gap between tax revenue coming from imports versus domestic transactions.
This divergence suggests that imports are contributing significantly to the overall growth in collections rather than local production.

Experts say this trend could warrant a reassessment of some production-linked incentive (PLI, government financial rewards given to companies for boosting domestic manufacturing) schemes to strengthen domestic manufacturing.
analysis.what_happened: India's tax collections hit Rs 2.04 lakh crore in September due to strong economic activity. However, experts noticed that a big chunk of this growth is coming from taxes collected on goods brought in from other countries (imports) rather than goods made inside India.
analysis.analogy: It is like a shop owner who thinks their business is booming, only to realize most of the cash register's earnings are coming from reselling items bought from outside wholesalers, rather than things made in their own workshop.
why_it_matters_india: Imports grow faster than domestic transactions -> tax revenue relies more heavily on foreign goods.
Higher reliance on imports -> experts suggest rethinking government support schemes like production-linked incentives (PLI).
Rethinking production incentives -> potential changes in how the government funds and supports local factories.
Stronger local manufacturing push -> impacts domestic industrial growth and self-reliance over time.

impacts.target: Industrial stocks and manufacturing companies in India
impacts.rationale: If experts push for a reassessment of manufacturing incentives due to heavy import reliance, local players might face policy shifts, which can create short-term uncertainty for investors.

impacts.target: Government tax revenue and fiscal health
impacts.rationale: Reaching Rs 2.04 lakh crore in September gives the government more money to spend on infrastructure and welfare, which is generally good for the economy.

watch_next: Any official government announcements regarding changes to production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes
Future monthly GST collection data to see if domestic transactions catch up with imports
analysis.caveats: Only the headline and a short excerpt were available, so the full depth of expert recommendations could not be verified.

events.headline: AI boom and trade resilience to Middle East crisis lift outlook, but gains to be uneven

items.title: AI boom and trade resilience to Middle East crisis lift outlook, but gains to be uneven
items.summary: Global trade proved more resilient than expected in the first half of 2026 despite the disruption caused by the Middle East conflict, as supply chains adapted and strong investment in artificial intelligence provided a powerful boost to goods trade. However, the resilience was not uniform, with services trade and some regions more exposed to the effects of the conflict. WTO economists have therefore raised the forecast for merchandise trade growth in 2026 while lowering the outlook for services trade.

events.article_text:
According to the latest "Global Trade Outlook and Statistics" released on 8 October, merchandise trade volume is now expected to grow by 3.9% in 2026, up from the March forecast of 1.9%, before increasing further to 4.1% in 2027 (see Chart 1). The revision reflects evidence that global supply chains adapted to disruptions in energy and fertilizer markets, while strong investment in AI-related infrastructure boosted trade in AI-enabling goods. Commercial services trade growth is expected to remain positive, although prospects have moderated due to the impact of the Middle East conflict on transport and international travel. Services trade volume is expected to grow by 3.3% in 2026, down from 4.8% in the March forecast, before rising by 6.4% in 2027.

Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said: "The numbers reflect trade resilience in action. When disruptions strike, an integrated world economy and a rules-based trading system provide economies flexibility to keep essential products flowing to businesses and households that need them. Nevertheless, some have felt the shock more than others, and not everyone can access emerging opportunities like AI. It is essential to ensure that the rules-based trading system continues to absorb shocks and bridge gaps so that opportunities are open to all."

Merchandise trade volume grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2026, exceeding expectations despite the disruption caused by the Middle East conflict. The performance reflected the ability of supply chains to adapt to shocks affecting energy, fertilizer and transport markets. Although crude oil exports from the Middle East fell by roughly 24% and liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports by 47% in the first half of 2026, increased shipments from other suppliers helped limit the decline in global exports to around 6% for crude oil and just 1% for LNG. Fertilizer markets also adjusted despite severe disruption, with global imports of nitrogenous fertilizers only 2.8% below recent averages and phosphatic fertilizer imports 2.2% higher as alternative suppliers stepped in. Meanwhile, trade flows were rerouted through alternative ports and corridors. Global container throughput remained resilient, rising 3.9% year-to-date through July.

Strong demand linked to AI investment more than offset the negative effects of the conflict in the Middle East. Demand for AI-enabling goods such as semiconductors and servers accounted for 47% of global merchandise trade growth in the first half of 2026, and trade in these products rose by 67% year-on-year, accelerating from the already rapid expansion seen in 2024 and 2025.

Commercial services trade grew by 14% year-on-year in value terms in the first quarter of 2026 and 10% in the second quarter. Growth slowed in the second quarter as the Middle East conflict disrupted transport and travel services, two sectors that depend heavily on the region's role as a global hub. Transport services were affected by the reorganization of shipping routes and sharply higher freight costs. Travellers' expenditure abroad increased by just 5% year-on-year in the second quarter, down from 15% in the first quarter. International tourist arrivals fell by 0.8% in the second quarter and were only 0.4% higher in the first half of the year overall according to data from the United Nations World Tourism Organization, reflecting a contraction in international tourist arrivals.

Despite these headwinds, other commercial services, particularly digitally delivered services, remained comparatively resilient and continued to support overall services trade growth. Computer services exports, one of the fastest-growing segments of services trade, rose by 18% year-on-year in the first quarter and an estimated 12% in the second quarter, helping to offset weakness in transport and travel services. Financial services exports likewise grew, by 14% year-on-year in the second quarter.

The report includes an analytical chapter on trade in AI-enabling goods, examining how the AI investment boom is reshaping global trade patterns, regional specialization and the geography of demand and supply.

Given stronger-than-expected merchandise trade growth in the first half of 2026, WTO economists now expect world merchandise trade volume to increase by 3.9% in 2026 and 4.1% in 2027, while global GDP growth is forecast at 2.6% and 2.9%, respectively (see Table 1).

AI-related investment is expected to remain a major driver of merchandise trade through 2027. Global AI infrastructure spending is projected to increase by at least 30% in 2026. Current market projections suggest AI capital expenditure will continue to rise by a further 10-20% in 2027. The conflict in the Middle East is expected to weigh on trade in 2026 through higher energy prices and disruptions to transport routes.

Regional trade prospects remain uneven. In 2026, Asia is expected to record the fastest merchandise export growth (9.9%), followed by North America (5.7%), Africa (5.6%) and South America (3.4%). Export performance is projected to remain weak in Europe (-0.1%) and to contract sharply in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) (-3.9%) and the Middle East (-17.2%), reflecting the impact of the ongoing conflict and associated disruptions to trade flows. On the import side, Asia (9.5%), Africa (8.9%) and the CIS (8.8%) are expected to post the strongest growth, while North America (1.4%) and Europe (0.5%) are likely to see only modest increases and the Middle East is forecast to record a steep decline (-15.4%).

The outlook for commercial services trade has weakened since the March forecast as the conflict in the Middle East continues to disrupt transport and travel services. WTO economists now expect commercial services trade volume to grow by 3.3% in 2026, down from the previous forecast of 4.8%, before rebounding to 6.4% in 2027 (see Table 2). analysis.tldr: A global boom in artificial intelligence and resilient supply chains are helping world trade grow faster than expected, which is a positive sign for India's technology and software service exports.
the_story: According to a World Trade Organization report released on 8 October, global merchandise trade volume is now expected to grow by 3.9% in 2026 (up from a March forecast of 1.9%) and 4.1% in 2027.

The upgrade is driven by a massive surge in demand for AI-enabling goods like semiconductors and servers, which rose 67% year-on-year and accounted for 47% of global merchandise trade growth in early 2026.
Global supply chains successfully adapted to severe Middle East conflict disruptions, replacing drops in regional oil and gas shipments with alternative suppliers and rerouting shipping corridors.
However, commercial services trade growth for 2026 was revised down to 3.3% because the Middle East conflict disrupted transport routes, shipping costs, and international travel.
Asia is projected to record the fastest merchandise export growth of any region in 2026, at 9.9%.
analysis.what_happened: The World Trade Organization raised its global trade growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027. This happened because global supply chains found new energy and fertilizer suppliers to bypass Middle East disruptions, and a massive investment boom in artificial intelligence created huge demand for technology hardware.
analysis.analogy: It is like a large delivery network where a few main roads get blocked by roadwork, but the drivers quickly find smart shortcuts and other highways, while a sudden massive rush for new computer parts keeps the delivery trucks busier than ever.
why_it_matters_india: Global demand for technology hardware and digital services accelerates -> Indian IT (Information Technology) and software service providers see steady foreign client spending.
Asia is expected to lead merchandise export growth at 9.9% in 2026 -> Indian manufacturing and export sectors stand to benefit from this broader regional trade expansion.
Middle East conflicts continue to disrupt transport and travel, raising shipping costs -> Imported goods and crude oil can face price pressures, affecting domestic costs.
Computer services exports globally rose 12% to 18% -> Reinforces India's strong position as a primary exporter of computer and digital services.

impacts.rationale: Strong global demand for digital services and computer exports supports business growth, which is generally good for tech sector investors.
Ongoing Middle East transport disruptions and higher shipping costs can push up import prices, making everyday goods slightly costlier—bad for consumers.
Higher global trade growth and robust Asian export performance generally improve overall business sentiment, which is good for equity markets.

watch_next: Updates on global semiconductor and AI infrastructure spending
Shipping costs and freight rate trends affected by Middle East transport routes
Export performance figures for Asian economies
analysis.caveats: The WTO report notes that if the Middle East conflict worsens further, it could escalate energy prices and disrupt transport enough to slow down these positive trade projections.

events.article_text:
Russia, Germany Add Diesel Supply as Fuel Market Scrambles for Barrels

What I Cover My focus spans the global energy landscape and the technologies reshaping it, specifically focusing on oil and gas, renewables, and tech-driven market…

Gasoline topped $4.40 a gallon in the U.S. in September, and Brent has sat above $100 a barrel since early September, up from around $60 before the Iran war started. Drivers have responded about how you'd expect. New hybrid sales in the U.S. rose 24% through the third quarter, battery-electric registrations jumped 52% across Europe in August, and the International Energy Agency figures EVs will make up nearly 30% of global car sales this year.

That should have been a gift to the electrification trade, but a Bloomberg gauge of 104 EV-linked companies is down 1% for the year, dragged lower by Tesla and BYD, and Albemarle, the biggest U.S. lithium name, closed at $102.75 on Oct. 7, less than half its 52-week high. The money coming out of this oil shock has been picky about where it lands, and a fair amount of it has landed on companies most people wouldn't file under "EV play" at all.

Earlier this year, Honda Motor Co. (NYSE: HMC) looked like one of the biggest casualties of the EV transition. The Japanese automaker booked more than $9 billion in costs to unwind its electric vehicle plans and posted its first annual loss in nearly 70 years, and CEO Toshihiro Mibe ended up apologizing to shareholders at the company's annual meeting in June. Honda's answer was to go all in on hybrids, with plans for 15 new hybrid models by 2030, mostly for North America, and the timing turned out to be close to perfect.

With gas north of $4, Honda sold more than 106,000 hybrids in the U.S. in the third quarter, a record, and hybrids now make up 53% of CR-V sales. CFO Masao Kawaguchi told reporters in August that rising fuel prices in North America were driving demand for its hybrids and fuel-efficient gas models, and the earnings back him up. Operating profit more than doubled to ¥530.8 billion in the April-to-June quarter, a record for any quarter in Honda's history, and the company raised its full-year operating profit forecast by 30% to ¥650 billion.

Not all of that is about oil, since a weaker yen and smaller tariff bills helped too, and Honda still expects about ¥520 billion in restructuring costs this year. Investors have warmed up anyway, sending the ADRs up more than 7% in May when Honda's guidance beat estimates. Honda didn't see this oil shock coming any more than anyone else did, but after spending billions backing out of EVs, it happened to have exactly the cars people wanted when gas went over $4.

ChargePoint Holdings Inc. (NYSE: CHPT) spent the last few years as a cautionary tale for EV charging investors, with a share price that kept sliding and a business that couldn't seem to stop losing money. Then came its Sept. 2 earnings report. Revenue rose 18% to $116.1 million, well ahead of guidance, the adjusted EBITDA loss shrank to $4.8 million from $22.1 million a year earlier, and the company burned essentially no cash in the quarter. The stock jumped more than 70% the next day.

CEO Rick Wilmer was pretty direct about what's behind it on the earnings call, pointing to U.S. gas at about $4.10 a gallon in late July, up roughly 31% from a year earlier, and saying the gap has "a direct impact on consumer purchasing decisions." Much of the beat came from home chargers sold in North America, which is about as clean a sign as you'll get that drivers are doing the math at the pump, even with the federal EV tax credit gone. Europe helped too, where Wilmer said EV sales rose 33% in July.

And then CFO Mansi Khetani poured a little cold water on it, calling those home charger sales lumpy and tied to events like Prime Day. ChargePoint guided third-quarter revenue to $105 million to $115 million, which works out to about 4% growth at the midpoint, it still loses money and it has roughly $96 million in cash. The shares also slid in early October as traders rotated into EVgo and Blink after an 82% monthly run. I'd want to see one more quarter like this before I believe the turnaround is real.

If you want a sense of how jumpy investors are about anything tied to the energy transition right now, look at SolarEdge Technologies Inc. (Nasdaq: SEDG). The inverter and home battery maker rallied almost 80% in May, then fell 24.6% in a single session after its second-quarter report in August, and it closed at $32.47 on Oct. 8, less than half where it traded in the spring.

The business underneath is in better shape than the chart, and Europe is the reason. SolarEdge's European revenue more than doubled from a year earlier in the second quarter, which management tied to households buying solar ahead of expected electricity price increases and adding batteries as several big markets phase out net metering. Battery shipments climbed to 426 megawatt-hours from 331 in the first quarter, and total revenue rose 20% to $346.2 million as the company posted its first non-GAAP operating profit since 2023.

What sank the stock was everything else: third-quarter guidance of $310 million to $340 million came in well short of what Wall Street wanted, U.S. residential demand is still soft after the federal solar credit expired, and the company has picked up a string of shareholder class-action investigations since September. It's a real European electrification story attached to a stock that trades like a coin flip.

Eaton Corp. (NYSE: ETN) is the least exciting name on this list and probably the safest. The power management giant makes the switchgear, panels and power electronics that sit between the grid and almost everything that gets electrified, and its second-quarter sales hit a record $8.5 billion, up 21%, with orders in its Electrical Americas business up 41% on a rolling 12-month basis. The stock set a new 52-week high after the report.

To be fair, most of that growth is coming from AI

analysis.tldr: When global oil prices surge past $100 a barrel, consumers rush toward electric vehicles and hybrids, creating unexpected windfalls for specific automotive and power-equipment companies.
the_story: Brent crude oil has stayed above $100 a barrel since early September, up from around $60 before the Iran war started, pushing U.S. gasoline past $4.40 a gallon.
Higher fuel costs drove up demand for fuel-efficient alternatives: U.S. hybrid sales rose 24% in the third quarter, and European battery-electric registrations jumped 52% in August.
Honda Motor Co. recorded a record operating profit of ¥530.8 billion in the April-to-June quarter and raised its full-year forecast by 30% after selling a record 106,000 hybrids in the U.S.
ChargePoint Holdings reported an 18% rise in revenue to $116.1 million and saw its stock jump over 70% following strong demand for home chargers as drivers reacted to expensive petrol.
Power management giant Eaton Corp. hit a record $8.5 billion in second-quarter sales, up 21%, driven by widespread grid electrification and artificial intelligence demand.
analysis.what_happened: Global oil prices shot up past $100 a barrel after an oil shock linked to the Iran war. With petrol becoming much more expensive, drivers worldwide rushed to buy hybrid and electric vehicles, boosting sales and profits for companies that sell fuel-efficient cars, home chargers, and electrical grid equipment.
analysis.analogy: It is like a sudden jump in the price of regular cooking gas forcing households to buy induction stoves, creating a rush to buy those stoves and the wiring needed to run them.
why_it_matters_india: Global oil shocks push up international crude prices.
As an oil importer, India faces a higher import bill for crude oil.
Costlier oil can weaken the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars) and push up domestic inflation (general rise in prices).
Global shifts toward electric vehicles and power equipment affect Indian auto component makers and renewable energy stocks.

impacts.rationale: Supply shocks keep oil prices elevated, which is bad for India as it increases import costs.
Higher oil import bills mean India needs more dollars, weakening the rupee—generally bad for everyday consumers as imports become pricier.
Expensive crude feeds into transport and goods costs, raising overall inflation—bad for household budgets.
Global shifts toward electric and hybrid vehicles can lift local auto suppliers exporting parts—good for investors in those sectors.

events.headline: Deep Sea Dreams

items.title: Deep Sea Dreams
items.summary: India is promoting deep-sea fishing with the promise of better incomes for the country’s traditional fishers. Government schemes have sought to accelerate this transition by providing financial support for deep-sea fishing vessels. Yet the move into deeper waters has proved far more complicated than policy documents suggest. Across the coastal states of India, fishing communities […]

events.article_text: India is promoting deep-sea fishing with the promise of better incomes for the country’s traditional fishers. Government schemes have sought to accelerate this transition by providing financial support for deep-sea fishing vessels. Yet the move into deeper waters has proved far more complicated than policy documents suggest. Across the coastal states of India, fishing communities are raising concerns about whether the economics of deep-sea fishing are actually feasible for India’s fishers. In several major fishing states, the government-backed schemes to promote deep-sea fishing have struggled to attract takers. This series follows the 2020-2025 phase of India’s deep sea fishing scheme and examines the country’s ambitions, the boats designed to make it possible, the growing focus on high-value species, and, most importantly, the realities faced by fishers being asked to invest in an uncertain future. Through months of field reporting and conversations with communities across India’s coastal states, Right to Information replies and Lok Sabha reports, Mongabay-India examines what it will take to keep India’s deep sea dreams afloat. This series was produced in partnership with the Pulitzer Center’s Ocean Reporting Network.

analysis.tldr: Government efforts to push traditional Indian fishers into deep-sea fishing face major hurdles, meaning the expected boost in coastal incomes may take much longer to materialize.
the_story: India is promoting deep-sea fishing with government schemes designed to give financial support for buying deep-sea fishing vessels and promise better incomes for traditional fishers.
Across various coastal states, fishing communities are worried about whether the economics of deep-sea fishing are actually feasible for local fishers.
Government-backed schemes to promote this transition have struggled to attract enough takers in several major fishing states.

A series by Mongabay-India, produced with the Pulitzer Center’s Ocean Reporting Network, examines the 2020-2025 phase of India's deep-sea fishing scheme through field reporting, Right to Information replies, and Lok Sabha reports.
analysis.what_happened: The Indian government is pushing traditional fishers to move into deep-sea fishing by offering financial support for specialized boats to catch high-value species. However, local fishing communities across coastal states are hesitant because they doubt the financial feasibility of the venture, causing government schemes to struggle with low participation.
analysis.analogy: It is like a government offering cash subsidies to small neighborhood grocery shop owners to buy massive delivery trucks, but the shop owners worry the daily fuel costs and maintenance will ruin them before they ever make a profit.
why_it_matters_india: Government policy pushes traditional fishers to invest in expensive deep-sea vessels.
Fishers face high financial uncertainty and low participation rates due to doubts about the economics.
Coastal state economies face slower-than-expected modernization in the fishing sector.
Incomes for traditional fishers remain constrained by the high cost of transitioning to deeper waters.

impacts.target: Coastal state economies and local fisher incomes
impacts.rationale: Slower uptake of deep-sea schemes means traditional fishers may not see the promised income boosts anytime soon, which is challenging for coastal livelihoods.

watch_next: Updates on the 2020-2025 phase of India's deep-sea fishing scheme
Responses from coastal fishing communities to revised government financial support
analysis.caveats: This card is based entirely on the published article text detailing the challenges faced by government deep-sea fishing schemes.

events.headline: East Asia’s manufacturing escalator has slowed – AI alone will not restart it

items.title: East Asia’s manufacturing escalator has slowed – AI alone will not restart it
items.summary: Exports of AI hardware are lifting regional growth, but the rules that decide who profits are being set without it.

events.article_text:
In Malaysia, data centres need RM4.6 million of investment for every job created (Amar Syazwan Rosman/Unsplash)

Exports of AI hardware are lifting regional growth, but the rules that decide who profits are being set without it.

East Asia’s manufacturing escalator has slowed – AI alone will not restart it

At the UN General Assembly last month, artificial intelligence (AI) was centre stage (Opens in new window). Brazil and France worried about power concentrated in a handful of firms and states. Developing countries asked for access to computing power, know-how and infrastructure, and for a real voice in setting standards to shape AI to fit their developmental needs. The United States treated AI dominance as a strategic and economic imperative.

Less than a week later, the World Bank’s October East Asia and Pacific Economic Update, “Riding the AI Wave” (Opens in new window), looked to identify benefits. While much of the world debates who will shape AI, East Asia is busy riding its wave. Putting the story together, it shows what AI export-oriented growth can and cannot do for emerging economies.

According to the World Bank, China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam exported US$1.4 trillion of AI-related goods in the 12 months to April. In early 2026, US imports of AI-enabling goods rose almost 60% while its other imports fell by nearly a quarter. AI-related exports from Vietnam and Malaysia have at least doubled from their 2020–22 average. The World Bank’s upgrade to the region’s 2026 growth forecast rests largely on these chips, servers and routers driven by a wave in AI investment.

A closer look at what is being exported is warranted. Assembled computers, servers and routers make up 69% of Thailand’s AI-related exports, and 60% of Vietnam’s. China’s AI-related exports of US$785 billion are mostly intermediates, much of it shipped to ASEAN countries for assembly. The design, software, intellectual property and data that make these goods valuable are largely created and captured elsewhere.

This is the familiar lesson of global value chains: what matters is which tasks a country performs, not which products it ships overseas.

When developing countries ask the UN for a voice in setting AI standards, they are making a trade policy demand too.

Manufacturing was not only good for exports, it used to be the escalator (Opens in new window) that moved workers off farms and into better-paid, more productive work. The World Bank is candid that this escalator has slowed.

Countries that reached their peak industrial employment share in 2015 and 2019 did so at incomes of roughly US$900 to US$5,900 per head, far short of high-income status. AI hardware does not change this. In Malaysia (Opens in new window), data centres need RM4.6 million of investment for every job created, against less than RM1 million in electronics and automotive jobs. Tellingly, when the World Bank looks for jobs at scale, it turns to tourism and agribusiness, not AI.

This is where services come in. Services (Opens in new window) already account for roughly 26–33% of the value of global manufactured exports. The report confirmed that services provide large support to the region’s growth, but it also conceded that its AI trade numbers miss AI-related services altogether: software development, business process outsourcing and data work.

This is precisely where the Philippines and Vietnam are building new capabilities. The report also cites Vietnam’s (Opens in new window)experience around its accession to the World Trade Organisation of opening telecommunications, finance and other services, which raised productivity not only in those sectors but in the manufacturing sectors that rely on them. Notably, while Vietnam still lags in services openness (Opens in new window) compared to other East Asian countries, it sees the export-led growth path through services capability, not around it.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei gives an on-screen presentation to the UN Security Council meeting on Artificial Intelligence and International Security, 23 September 2026 (Manuel Elías/UN Photo)

Which brings us back to New York. The UNGA debate focused on safety, ethics and access, all real concerns. But the economic terms of the AI economy are being set somewhere else, and mostly outside multilateral forums.

The region’s AI export boom rests on unilateral decisions of importing markets. Most AI-related goods remain exempt from US tariffs. What is granted unilaterally can be withdrawn unilaterally. The boom also rests on an investment cycle, with the largest US hyperscalers spending more than US$1 trillion over 2025 and 2026, which the World Bank warns could reverse if it proves to have run ahead of demand.

Meanwhile, the rules that will decide who captures value from AI – on cross-border data flows, digitally delivered services, standards and export controls – are being written unilaterally or at best in bilateral and mini plurilateral deals and national security reviews. Most developing countries have little say in any of them.

So what still should work for emerging economies as their growth drivers? Openness still works, but openness to services, technology and ideas now matters more than cheap labour and economies of scale. Countries need to compete on tasks rather than sectors, invest in physical and digital connectivity and skills, and reform services regulation so that their manufacturers and digital exporters can draw on efficiently provided inputs. And they need to treat the multilateral rulebook as something worth fighting for: not because it is perfect, but because the alternative is a world in which the terms are set by the few with the most compute.

East Asia has shown, once again, that it can build what the world wants to buy. The harder task is making sure it also has a hand in writing the rules under which it is sold. And, just as crucially, it must put more of what it builds to work at home.

Mia Mi

analysis.tldr: East Asia's AI hardware boom creates lots of physical goods but surprisingly few local jobs, showing India that relying solely on manufacturing assembly won't automatically solve employment challenges.
the_story: According to the World Bank, countries like China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam exported US$1.4 trillion of AI-related goods in the 12 months leading up to April.

US imports of AI-enabling goods rose by almost 60% in early 2026, while its other imports dropped by nearly a quarter, and Vietnam and Malaysia's AI exports at least doubled from their 2020-22 average.
Most of these exports are assembled computers, servers, and routers (69% in Thailand, 60% in Vietnam), while high-value design, software, and intellectual property are created elsewhere.

The traditional manufacturing escalator has slowed down; for example, data centres in Malaysia need RM4.6 million of investment for every single job created, compared to less than RM1 million for electronics and automotive jobs.
The World Bank warns that the current AI export boom relies heavily on US import exemptions and a US$1+ trillion investment cycle by big tech firms that could reverse if demand cools.
analysis.what_happened: East Asian countries are experiencing a massive surge in exporting AI-related hardware like chips, servers, and routers, driven by heavy US demand and tech investments. However, the World Bank points out that this hardware boom creates very few jobs locally because most high-value tasks like design and software happen elsewhere, and traditional manufacturing no longer easily lifts masses of workers into well-paid jobs.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local factory getting a huge contract to assemble fancy smartphones, but the foreign company keeps all the design patents, software profits, and engineering jobs for themselves, leaving the local workers with low-margin assembly work.
why_it_matters_india: East Asian export boom -> Shows that shipping physical tech hardware brings high revenue numbers but fails to generate mass employment.
Shift toward services and software value -> Highlights why India's existing focus on IT services, software development, and digital outsourcing aligns with where global productivity is moving.
Risk of unilateral global trade rules -> Reminds emerging markets that heavy reliance on foreign buyers can be disrupted if importing countries suddenly change tariffs or investment trends.
Need for domestic digital adoption -> Emphasizes that developing nations must put their tech capabilities to work at home rather than just exporting components.

impacts.rationale: Global emphasis on digital services and software tasks could eventually benefit Indian IT exporters, which is good for tech investors.
More efficient global technology and digital inputs can lower costs for businesses, helping keep consumer price increases gentle.

watch_next: Whether major importing countries like the US introduce new tariffs or rules on AI hardware and digital services
How developing economies shift their focus toward boosting services and domestic technology adoption
analysis.caveats: The article focuses primarily on East Asia and the Pacific, so direct policy impacts on India depend entirely on how Indian policymakers choose to adapt their own manufacturing and services strategies.

events.headline: Awkward: Saudi Arabia’s new EV brand takes on the U.S. rival it already controls

items.title: Awkward: Saudi Arabia’s new EV brand takes on the U.S. rival it already controls
items.summary: The Exobot SUV by Ceer Motors

events.article_text:
Saudi Arabia’s first homegrown electric-vehicle maker is set to take on a U.S. rival the kingdom already controls.

Ceer Motors, majority-owned by the sovereign Public Investment Fund, revealed two electric car models on September 21, with deliveries promised for March 2027. The EVs were designed and engineered in Saudi Arabia, and will be built at Ceer’s plant in King Abdullah Economic City, north of Jeddah.

This is the PIF’s third EV bet. It bought about 5% of Tesla in 2018 and sold almost all of it by the end of 2019. It has also put about $8 billion into California-based Lucid, which has never turned a profit.

For the U.S., Ceer’s debut sets up an awkward rivalry: Saudi Arabia is building its own EV brand while its sovereign wealth fund owns a majority stake in Lucid, whose main factory is in Arizona. Ceer is PIF’s hedge against Lucid, whose shares have slumped more than 60% this year and whose Saudi sales are shrinking in a market dominated by China’s BYDiBYDBYD Auto is a Chinese carmaker that became the world’s leading EV manufacturer in 2023, competing with Tesla for market share and global attention.READ MORE.

“Lucid is an existing global technology and luxury-EV company in which Saudi Arabia has invested heavily,” Bill Russo, founder and CEO of Shanghai-based consulting firm Automobility, told Rest of World. “Ceer has a different mandate, creating a Saudi automotive OEM [original equipment manufacturer] and, importantly, an indigenous industrial ecosystem.”

Ceer, a venture between PIF and Taiwanese electronics maker Foxconn, was launched in November 2022. It had set 2025 as the target for its first cars.

Last week, the company’s CEO, James DeLuca, said Ceer will begin production early next year. Ceer has planned more models over the next five years, the company said at the launch. It also aims to make almost half the components of its cars locally by 2034.

Ceer’s Exobot sedan and an SUV are high-powered premium EVs — the segment where Lucid sells its Air luxury sedan and Gravity SUV. The most powerful Exobot versions promise more than 1,100 horsepower, DeLuca said, close to the 1,234 horsepower of Lucid’s fastest car, the Air Sapphire sedan. Ceer has yet to announce prices.

“That does put the initial products closer to Lucid’s premium territory than to BYD’s mass-market center of gravity,” Russo said.

The real test of its strategy will come when that range broadens, Russo said. Lucid, in which PIF holds about 58%, is already badly weakened. This year, it named a new CEO, Silvio Napoli; cut about a fifth of its U.S. workforce; ended its second production shift in Arizona; and recalled 27,000 sedans over a fire risk. Its market value has shrunk to about $1.6 billion.

In Saudi Arabia, Lucid’s sales fell 57% in the first seven months of 2026, while BYD’s rose 369%, according to estimates from Focus2Move, a Rome-based firm that tracks car sales in more than 150 countries. The gap partly reflects price, Hashim AlFatayerji, CEO of the independent Saudi advisory firm Cararak, told Rest of World.

“BYD and Lucid serve very different segments, so comparing their volumes directly can be misleading,” AlFatayerji said.

PIF has kept faith with Lucid through the slump. The carmaker remains one of only five U.S. companies in the fund’s latest quarterly holdings filing, and the Saudi government has agreed to buy up to 100,000 Lucid vehicles over 10 years.

Saudi Arabia has no official count of EV sales. Saudis buy almost 1 million new vehicles a year, and 10,000 to 20,000 of them are electric, AlFatayerji estimated. Joseph Salem, a senior partner who heads travel, transport, and hospitality at consulting firm Arthur D. Little in the Middle East and North Africa, puts the figure at 35,000 to 40,000 EVs in 2025, not counting plug-in hybrids.

Ceer’s factory is designed for as many as 240,000 vehicles a year, and Lucid already runs a smaller plant in the kingdom. That is far more than Saudi buyers can take, Salem told Rest of World.

“Combined, their full-capacity targets are roughly 10 times what the domestic market can plausibly absorb near-term,” he said. “So the majority of output, I’d say 80% plus, has to be export-oriented almost by design.”

Saudi Arabia is building a car industry sized for the Gulf, North Africa, and beyond, backed by PIF money and trade access across the region, Salem said. Exporting is the strategy, he said.

“The domestic market is the proving ground, not the end goal,” Salem said.

60% of the electric cars sold in the Middle East are from China’s BYD.

Abroad, Ceer will meet Chinese rivals that already lead the region. In the Middle East, BYD sells about 60% of electric cars and Tesla about 15%, according to the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook.

Chinese carmakers pose a tougher test, Russo said. They have spent years building huge factories, close ties with suppliers, and the ability to sell cheaply, and are now expanding abroad because they can make more cars than China can absorb, he said.

Ceer relies on established suppliers for key parts. Its motors come from Croatia’s Rimac and South Korea’s Hyundai Transys, while its platform is from Taiwan’s Foxconn. It has licensed some component technology from BMW.

“A new entrant cannot simply license its way to that level of competitiveness,” Russo said.

To win buyers at home and abroad, Ceer must match BYD on price, using local parts and state-backed financing, Salem said. It also needs a dealer and service network as wide as BYD’s from the outset, and cars that stand out on their own merits beyond being made in Saudi Arabia, he said.

“It’s a high bar,” Salem said. “But Ceer has the capital and policy backing to close that gap faster than a typical new entrant would.”

Ceer has advantages few new carmakers get, including long-term funding, a powerful backer at home, and the freedom to build on proven technology from others, said Russo. What it still has to earn is a brand that wins customers on

analysis.tldr: Saudi Arabia launching its own electric car brand increases global competition in the electric vehicle market, which could eventually lead to cheaper battery and car technologies for Indian consumers.

analysis.what_happened: Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund is backing a new electric car company called Ceer Motors to build vehicles locally. analysis.analogy: It is like a wealthy mall owner who already bought a franchise store that is struggling, but decides to open their own competing local shop next door just to make sure they control the market no matter what.
why_it_matters_india: Saudi Arabia's push to build global electric vehicle manufacturing adds more deep-pocketed players to the worldwide supply chain.

history.title: The fastest crash and the fastest rescue
history.what: Global shares fell about 35% in five weeks — the fastest crash of that size ever recorded. Then, within months, they made new highs, while the real economy was still shut.
history.why: A genuine shock met an economy with no slack. But the crash's speed came from its mechanics: everything was sold at once to raise cash, including gold and government bonds. The rescue's speed came from central banks having the 2008 playbook ready and choosing to use it at a scale and pace nobody expected.
history.impact: India's Nifty fell 38% in a month and recovered within the year. Oil futures briefly traded below zero. Meanwhile millions lost work and informal economies were devastated — the gap between the market and the economy was the widest most investors had ever seen.
history.policy: Interest rates to near zero, unlimited bond buying, and — the genuine novelty — enormous direct fiscal transfers to households and firms. Money was put into people's hands rather than only into the banking system, which is what 2008 had done.
history.consequence: The recovery was far faster than after 2008, and the inflation that followed in 2021-23 was far larger — the first serious inflation in the rich world in forty years, and the reason interest rates rose so sharply afterwards. It also drew a whole generation of new retail investors into markets, in India especially, whose first experience was a V-shaped recovery.
history.pattern: Markets price the future, not the present. They bottomed while the news was at its worst because the rescue was visible before the recovery was. Waiting for the news to improve means buying after the move.
history.india_echo: India's retail investing boom dates from this crash — SIP accounts and demat openings multiplied. Most of that money has never seen a long bear market, which is a genuine risk factor for Indian small and mid caps.
history.watch_for: A policy response arriving faster than the damage. When the rescue is credible and immediate, the market stops waiting for the data.
